claim: Oil-based Vitamin D vehicle produced 4.05 nmol/L per 100 IU/day increase in 25(OH)D, compared to 2.75 for powder-based and 0.5 for ethanol — establishing oil vehicles as superior for D3 bioavailability.
stance_target: oil-carrier supplements (softgels, liquid drops) absorb D3 better than dry tablets
scope_conditions: Systematic review of 4 clinical studies, healthy subjects and mildly deficient populations; Mol Nutr Food Res 2010
quoted_support: When the information from these study populations was combined, oil-soluble vehicles produced the greatest rate of change in mean serum 25(OH)D per 100 000 IU, followed by powder-based vehicles and vitamin D dissolved in ethanol (4.05, 2.75, 0.5 nmol/L per 100 IU/day, respectively).

claim: Oil vehicle produced 4.25 times greater 25(OH)D increase than ethanol vehicle at 2000 IU average daily dose (Maalouf et al.), the only statistically significant vehicle comparison found.
stance_target: oil carrier dramatically outperforms non-lipid vehicles for D3 absorption
scope_conditions: Adolescents (aged 10-17, n=25), weekly 14,000 IU D3, 8-week study; Maalouf et al. 2008
quoted_support: Maalouf et al. compared the absorption of crystalline vitamin D3 dissolved in pharmaceutical grade ethanol to the absorption of D3 dissolved in Vigantoil, a medium-chain fatty acid supplement... They found that the oil vehicle produced a 4.25 times greater increase in serum 25(OH)D levels than the ethanol vehicle.

claim: Vitamin D3 absorption requires bile acid release triggered by fat in the duodenum, and D3 must associate with lipid micelles for intestinal uptake — mechanistically explaining why oil vehicles improve absorption.
stance_target: physiological mechanism supporting oil-based D3 formulation superiority
scope_conditions: General physiological absorption mechanism, as per review authors
quoted_support: The presence of fat in the duodenum stimulates the release of bile acids to facilitate lipid absorption. Vitamin D may require other lipids to stimulate the release of bile acids and with which to associate in micelles to facilitate its absorption by the intestinal mucosa. Therefore, vitamin D may exhibit differential efficacy in absorption when solubilized in oil, lactose powders, cellulose powders or ethanol.

claim: Fish oil capsule D3 produced 1.13x greater 25(OH)D increase than multivitamin cellulose tablet at 400 IU/day (non-significant), and lactose tablet produced 1.09x more than oil D2 (non-significant) — differences between powder and oil vehicles were modest and not statistically significant in two studies.
stance_target: magnitude of bioavailability difference between softgel/oil and powder tablets may be smaller than often claimed
scope_conditions: Holvik et al. 2007 (n=55, healthy adults, 400 IU D3); Saadi et al. 2007 (n=88, healthy females, 2000 IU D2)
quoted_support: The fish oil supplement produced an increase in mean serum 25(OH)D that was 1.13 times as great as the increase produced by the multivitamin supplement, a result that was not statistically significant... Saadi et al. found that the daily lactose tablet produced mean 25(OH)D levels 1.09 times the monthly supplement in the oil vehicle, but the difference was not statistically significant.
